speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This Motion is future-facing and strategic, because transport is about connectivity across three domains – land, sea and air – and connectivity enables economic prosperity that ultimately is about improving lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Day-to-day land transport issues remain important and a priority to the Transport GPC.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But they are not the focus of today's debate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: To be clear, the GPC firmly recognises that day-to-day public transport issues affect Singaporeans' everyday lives and their importance cannot be understated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But we have discussed these issues many times in and out of this House, and will continue to have ample opportunities to do so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A number were raised during the Land Transport Bill in February this year and I expect further Sittings later this year will address them too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I therefore urge honourable colleagues to focus this debate on what is set out in today's Motion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For this Motion, I will begin by setting the context and putting forth a few recommendations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: My GPC colleagues will in turn address the different tenets of the statement in greater detail.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: And I welcome more perspectives and ideas from other honorable colleagues speaking today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I would also like to take this chance to thank our Transport GPC resource panel, who took time to share their experiences and suggestions, which offered us different perspectives to consider when preparing for this debate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: History offers no clearer proof of transport infrastructure as destiny than the railway age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Albuquerque in New Mexico is a good example.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In 1880, the first train pulled in, connecting the town to major cities and trade networks, bringing a wave of opportunities that transformed it almost overnight.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Around the new station, hotels, cafes, warehouses and small factories flourished, creating opportunities for workers and entrepreneurs alike.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: At sea and in the air, Dubai tells the same story.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A fishing village became a global hub by treating each mode of connectivity as a building block for the next.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: By the 1830s, Singapore overtook Batavia as the centre of regional trade, linking the Chinese, Southeast Asian and European-Indian Ocean trading networks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: One decision to be a free port turned a fishing settlement into a regional emporium within a generation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: By 1980, Paya Lebar Airport was handling over seven million passengers a year, far beyond what the site could accommodate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Today, it connects over 170 cities, anchoring Singapore's position as a logistics and business hub entirely disproportionate to our size.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Ensuring multi-route and multi-modal connectivity matters more than ever in today's uncertain geopolitical climate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Because in an uncertain world, resilience is not measured by size, it is measured by how many ways we have to get through.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Thus, a small country like ours need to have strong, multiple connections as the foundation of our national resilience.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Global geopolitical shocks have always had an impact on Singapore, but increasingly so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The Russia-Ukraine war caused supply chain disruption, energy crunch and inflation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: US tariffs disrupted our export-oriented economy as multinational corporations (MNCs) reconfigured their supply chains.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: And most recently, the conflict affecting the Strait of Hormuz triggered energy price spikes, regional port congestion and inflated marine insurance costs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Singapore needs options to stay connected, to keep goods and people flowing in and out, whatever the disruption.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Ironically, the recent geopolitical situation along the Strait of Hormuz has also increased global reliance on the Strait of Malacca, where we are strategically situated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This represents both opportunity and risk for us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We must have the capacity and the capability to handle the rising flows, or we risk chokepoints and losing trade to other ports.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This means working more closely with neighbours in the region so that we can manage trade volume and storage demands together and achieve a win-win outcome for all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Singapore's transport system must be adaptive and responsive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The critical success factors for achieving it are three: frontier technologies, international cooperation and world-class infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Together, they serve one ultimate goal – generating and anchoring meaningful jobs for Singaporeans to take up and grow in.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As the world digitalises and frontier technologies scale, Singapore cannot afford to lag in adoption.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: At its core, leveraging frontier technology is about orchestration, predictability and efficiency.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It is about throughput, reliability and orchestration across a small, dense node sitting on major trade lanes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: AI's biggest contribution is not automating individual vehicles or terminals in isolation, it is making the whole system – port, airport, roads, warehouses, customs – all behaving as one coordinated network instead of separate silos.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Initiatives such as OCEANS-X and the Maritime Digital Twin are strong building blocks toward this vision.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This includes using AI to calculate tighter vessel-berthing configurations so that more ships can park safely within the same limited space.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: On autonomous vehicles (AVs), AVs are the physical execution layer for AI orchestration.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Together, this combination lets Singapore compress turnaround times and run operations 24/7, increasing our ports' effective capacity without expanding their footprint.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Today, AV adoption is most advanced at Tuas Port and in our maritime domain.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As we scale our experience with AI and AVs there, we should also extend this cautiously to other domains to complement existing services and fill gaps.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The Ministry of Transport (MOT) has made commendable progress in meaningfully deploying frontier technologies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But more can be done to harness this power and extend Singapore's advantage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I therefore call on the Ministry to consider: Number one, beef up on research and development (R&D) into AI applications and AI governance across land, sea and air transport.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This means greater investment in funding and in expertise, with transport innovation established as a key pillar of our national strategy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Given our hub status, and with the right infrastructure and governance, we can build rich, live datasets and applications that generate innovative transport solutions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: These solutions will not only benefit Singapore's own growth; they can be exported to other countries, enhancing interoperability, because if our partners adopt them, we are, in effect, operating on the same system and the same standards.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As we build higher-quality data and stronger digital twin systems for our ports, airports and logistics network, disruptions such as storms, cyberattacks, geopolitical chokepoint closures can be simulated and rerouted close to real time rather than leaving us on the back foot when they hit.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Today, our AI gains sit largely within single domains – land, sea or air – operating on their own.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: What would be transformative is linking the Maritime Digital Twin, an airport twin and a land network twin into one system, using AI to orchestrate genuinely intermodal decisions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This integration raises the potential for agentic AI – autonomous agents that orchestrate and make decisions on their own.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This is likely still some way off, as agentic governance has not been fully worked through.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But more research and experimentation are needed before we can confidently deploy such agents in transport, where the consequences of error carry real physical risk.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This means deliberate effort to preserve human oversight and to create meaningful jobs for our people – a point that I will return to later.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: My colleague Mr Edward Chia will speak more on the use of AI in the region and corresponding support for small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Likewise, Mr Jackson Lam will speak more on building the smartest integrated hub leveraging the technology and Mr Ang Wei Neng will speak on the deployment of AVs in transport.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Global connectivity is only possible if other countries are willing to interact and operate under the same rules and standards, or at least a common understanding.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This is what instils confidence and delivers efficiency.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Common standards enable interoperability and interoperability delivers efficiency.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But a ship, an aircraft or a container only benefits from Singapore's efficiency if the country on the other end recognises our clearances, honours the same safety standards and trusts that any dispute arising here will be resolved fairly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Many agreements and technical standards covering safety and operations are already in place.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But this is continuous work, especially as we digitalise: data standards, secure cross-border data governance; bridging the uneven maturity of digital trade documents, such as the bill of lading; and cyber incident reporting specific to transport – are examples to name a few.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As the world risks fragmenting further, with the United States (US) pulling back from multilateral engagement, there is a renewed and urgent imperative for Singapore, alongside other smaller states, to stand together to uphold the rule of law.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This demands skilled statecraft and sustained effort to engage and negotiate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But closer to home, we must also ensure our ties and agreements with our neighbours remain strong.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Because as a regional bloc, we carry far greater global weight together than any of us do alone.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Singapore must continue to take the lead in pushing for this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Here, I call on the Ministry to consider: First, pushing harder for international cooperation, especially within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: What can this House expect to see tabled at the regional meetings?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For this integration to succeed safely, particularly with AI agents as a possible future feature, we need robust governance, including sovereign data governance, AI governance and certification standards for autonomous decision-making, developed in step with the technology and in context of transport.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: My colleague Mr Sharael Taha will speak more on international leadership and standards setting and Singapore as an orchestrator in ASEAN.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Given everything I have said so far, it is clear that infrastructure today cannot be purely physical, nor purely digital.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We need hybrid infrastructure that integrates digital capability directly into the physical build.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: New projects will, of course, be hybrid by design.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But we must also upgrade our existing infrastructure, so that both old and new hard infrastructure can collect data to enable real-time prediction and intervention, so that the digital twins we rely on are not limited to historical data, but stay live to dynamic, real-world conditions as they happen.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: From optimising berthing and warehouse capacity, to developing a "digital freight corridor" linking port, airport and warehousing with shared real-time visibility as AVs move cargo from port to destination, these outcomes are only achievable if our physical infrastructure can keep pace with the software and AI agents running on top of it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Here, my question is: what more will MOT do to upgrade or build future-ready hybrid infrastructure so that Singapore is well placed to continue being a global hub?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Beyond hybrid infrastructure within our own borders, we should also look beyond Singapore's immediate geographical bounds, extending our hub function into complementary cities and ports across the ASEAN region, to cope with overflow demand while keeping the highest-margin activities here at home.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The Singapore-Johor-Riau Islands (SIJORI) approach has served us well and continues to be upgraded today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Building on this, the same model could arguably extend to other parts of the region.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Though we will need to carefully consider what stays in Singapore and what is better sited elsewhere, so that the arrangement remains mutually beneficial.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: My colleague Mr Liang Eng Hwa will speak more about building infrastructure to support the electrification and digitalisation of land transport and to connect Singapore and Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As we pursue all of the above, we should expect increased flows of goods and people, even as we must meet our green commitments to decarbonise.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The topic on sustainability must thus be considered.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: My colleague Ms Poh Li San will be speaking more on sustainability and specifically about positioning Singapore as an "International Green Air Hub".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Singapore has made admirable progress on sustainable aviation fuel.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But more can be done to diversify both the sources of our transport fuels and the routes through which we import them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Diversifying the sources of green fuel is a matter for our overall trade and energy strategy, and not one for this debate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But transport is directly relevant, because we must find ways to secure the transport of green energy itself to power Singapore's transport sector and indeed, every other national need.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Transport must be part of our national resilience strategy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The ASEAN Power Grid is a good example of a regional initiative that optimises the matching of green energy supply and demand across the region, but it carries risks that we must be prepared for.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Cambodia and Indonesia have abundant green energy – solar and hydro.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But transporting that energy to Singapore through conventional undersea cables, which was the best option we had, leaves us exposed to extrinsic risks, such as possible regional conflict and maritime accidents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As I said at the outset, all of these efforts to strengthen Singapore's global connectivity in logistics, maritime and aviation exist to secure our long-term economic competitiveness, which, ultimately, is about creating good opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: My colleague Ms Yeo Wan Ling will speak more on this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The development of these domains must therefore translate into higher-value jobs that Singaporeans can take up competently and confidently.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It employs around 170,000 people today and is entering a new phase where automation and AI are not eliminating jobs so much as elevating them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As public and private maritime investment grows, we should also expect real demand for Singaporean talent in maritime R&D, data science and technology commercialisation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The scaling of AI points to a new generation of maritime careers – higher-skilled, better-paid and built around the very technologies reshaping this industry globally.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But for this to succeed, we must equip and support current and future workers in land, sea and air transport with the right skills and training.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: AVs and smart equipment, for instance, often run on proprietary software or contain parts requiring specialised handling.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: So, the job opportunities are there but our workers need to be trained to take them up.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We must also do more to attract Singaporeans into these careers – raising awareness in schools and building meaningful career pathways.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Private sector players need to work more closely with our schools to ensure skills match market demand, and schools need to adapt their curriculum with agility to keep pace with technological change.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: AI is a good example of just how fast that pace can be – new models emerge within months and entire capabilities can shift direction just as quickly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: When Anthropic introduced a new feature called "skills" for its Claude AI in October 2025, it let AI follow specialised, step-by-step instructions for particular tasks, instead of figuring things out from scratch each time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It sounds like a small change, but it meant these tools could suddenly be trusted to handle more complex work on their own.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If our curriculum cannot keep pace with shifts like this, our workers risk being trained for yesterday's technology.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A related feedback from our GPC Resource Panel was the need for competency frameworks and curriculum to be reviewed and refreshed regularly, and to do so without being weighed down by conventional approval processes that could take up to a year.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: By the time such approval comes through, the technology will already have moved on.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Third, engaging students earlier, so they are equipped with the right information before they enter our IHLs and choose their course or specialisation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the Motion that we debate today seeks to explore how Singapore can consolidate its position as a globally connected aviation, maritime and logistics hub through international cooperation, frontier technologies and the building of world-class infrastructure, thereby strengthening our long-term economic competitiveness and creating more and better jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In the face of a rapidly shifting geopolitical landscape and the disruption brought by emerging technologies, Singapore must rethink how to maintain the deep connectivity with the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This Motion seeks to examine transport across all three domains – the land, sea and air – through a strategic lens.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: There is this ancient saying, "As a mirror, history can show you the rise and fall of dynasties." Throughout history, there is no shortage of examples of cities and states that grew prosperous through connectivity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For example, in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian: Account of the Moneymakers, he explicitly identified cities, such as Linzi, Handan, Wan, Luoyang and Han, as "great metropolises" and pointed out that the root of their wealth lies precisely in their position as transport hubs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Handan, connected northwards to Yan and Zhuo cities and southwards to Zheng and Wei cities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Linzi was a great metropolis between the sea and mountains; and Luoyang traded eastwards with Qi and Lu and southwards with Liang and Chu cities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: He further explained that when the Han dynasty unified the realm, it opened the passes and bridges and lifted restrictions on mountains and marshes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Thus, wealthy merchants and great traders circulated throughout the land and there was nothing that could not be traded.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The Grand Canal also offered another good example.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It gave rise to celebrated cities, such as Yangzhou, Huai'an, Jining and Linqing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In short, once a unified state removes the barriers between the passes and bridges, merchants and travellers can then move freely, and cities flourished as a result.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Global connectivity is a matter of survival and development for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We now live in an era of profound geopolitical uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Ensuring multi-route, multi-modal connectivity has never been so important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As a small nation lacking in natural resources, having robust and diversified channels of global connectivity is key to maintaining our national resilience.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Today, Singapore has much to be proud of in international cooperation, the adoption of new technologies and building of high-quality infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But we must look to redouble our efforts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Embracing these frontier technologies can also help us simulate better scenarios so that we can be better prepared to meet challenges and improve precision and foresight and therefore, enhance our efficiency and productivity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This is not about building a talent pipeline and reserve for the land, sea and air transport sectors, but also about helping Singaporeans seize more valuable opportunities. : Mr Speaker, Singapore did not inherit our connectivity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We built it deliberately, chapter by chapter, and this House now holds the pen for the next one.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Frontier technology, international cooperation and world-class hybrid infrastructure are the critical success factors that will cement Singapore's position as a global logistics, maritime and aviation hub and in turn determine whether we sustain our economic competitiveness and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Motion today calls on this House to affirm the critical importance of strengthening Singapore's long-term economic competitiveness by leveraging international cooperation, frontier technologies and world-class infrastructure to reinforce our position as a globally connected aviation, maritime and logistics hub and to anchor good jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I start with the standard of competitiveness and the changing horizon.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We are not blessed with natural resources, a massive domestic hinterland nor an expansive geographical footprint.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Capitalising on our geographical position, continuous investments and sustained developmental efforts since Independence have allowed us to establish Singapore as both a maritime and aviation hub.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Concurrently, Changi Airport has steadily recovered from the severe travel freezes of the COVID-19 pandemic, returning to high volumes of passenger traffic and air freight processing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We are now working on mega projects, such as the Tuas Port and Changi T5.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But Mr Speaker, past operational success does not guarantee resilience against future structural changes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Competition in logistics, aviation and maritime operations is moving away from purely physical throughput towards ownership of the software, data systems and digital platforms that orchestrate these global movements.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, value is rapidly shifting to the owners of global vessel tracking networks and automated AI logistic platforms rather than the physical ports they connect.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As we debate this Motion on preserving our long-term competitiveness, we must continue to evaluate the structural vulnerabilities underlying our transport hub status.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must actively fight to defend our share of the high value supply chain, ensuring that these digital and analytical segments remain anchored in Singapore rather than losing ground to rival digital hubs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If we focus solely on physical asset efficiency, we risk watching the true values of the global supply chain migrate to digital capitals elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, the geopolitical crucible – regional disputes and hub resilience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our long-term economic competitiveness cannot be divorced from our immediate geopolitical resilience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The past half a year has thrown our trade dependencies into sharp relief.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The crisis has once again demonstrated how quickly geopolitical shocks can reverberate through international trade networks and affect interconnected economies, like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For the first time in recent memory, global maritime and aviation corridors have faced simultaneous closures.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must look closely at how these multimodal disruptions have impacted Singapore over the past six months to extract vital lessons for our future survival.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, the maritime hub – energy shocks and equipment contagion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The closure of Hormuz has sent severe shock waves through our maritime transshipment and bunkering operations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: First, the immediate halts of outbound crude oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the Persian Gulf triggered an unprecedented global energy price shock.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This inflated fuel costs rapidly, introducing extreme price volatility that severely squeezed carrier margins.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Second, although primary East-West container shipping routes do not depend directly on the Persian Gulf, the conflict has nevertheless created significant knock-on effects across global logistics networks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Thousands of containers become stranded within affected regional supply chains, reducing equipment availability and disrupting normal cargo flows.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As carriers rapidly reshuffled schedules, redeployed vessels and adjusted service networks, major transshipment hubs faced the challenge of accommodating irregular arrival patterns and maintaining operational reliability amid heightened uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) can accelerate strategies to anchor alternative multimodal trade corridors and aggressively diversify our bunkering and energy supply networks away from traditional geopolitical checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: PSA can continually expand its dynamic yard capacity planning and utilise predictive AI tools to act as a reliable shock absorber when global schedules collapse.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, the air hub space constraints and a rerouting penalty.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Parallel to the maritime shocks, extensive air space restrictions across parts of the Middle East have fundamentally reconfigured international aviation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The disruption has affected airline scheduling, fleet deployment and the operational efficiency of several major aviation hubs, like Dubai and Doha.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The episode has also demonstrated the value of maintaining a resilient and globally connected aviation hub.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As airlines adjusted flight paths and network strategies to navigate operational uncertainties, Changi Airport and Singapore Airlines (SIA) were well positioned to capture the traffic opportunities arising from disruptions elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This reinforces the importance of operational flexibility and strong airline partnerships so that Singapore remains capable of responding rapidly when competing aviation corridors face disruptions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, these traffic flows come with operational challenges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To strengthen our air hub during periods of crisis, the Changi Airport Group (CAG) or MOT can consider targeted support measures to help carriers manage exceptional operational disruptions, while SIA can continue maintaining the fleet flexibility necessary to redeploy capacity rapidly across regions as circumstances evolve.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For the rest of my speech, I will be concentrating on certain issues affecting our maritime and logistics hubs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, the strategic vulnerability – the adopter versus creator gap.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While handling geopolitical crises requires tactical agility, solving our core structural bottleneck requires a profound policy shift across our maritime and logistics sectors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When overseas firms developed advanced cargo hardware or automated systems, Singapore is usually the first to integrate and run them efficiently.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our state-backed operators excel at deploying capital to operationalise foreign innovations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But let us ask an uncomfortable question: who owns the core software system?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The stark reality is that many local ship managers, airlines, freight forwarders and logistics operators continue to rely heavily on foreign-developed software platforms for critical operational functions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In shipping, it includes emissions monitoring and regulatory compliance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Operators rely on European systems, like Norway's Kongsberg.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The management layer is dominated by Western or North Asian tech conglomerates.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For voyage planning and fleet optimisation, the industry defaults to platforms like America's Veson nautical, vessel and asset management and also supply chain visibility in cargo tracking, and in this, the management layer is dominated by Western or North Asian tech conglomerates.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Across much of the global transport sector, the highest value software architects, data platforms and proprietary algorithms remain concentrated in major technology centres outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the modern digital economy, physical assets are increasingly becoming commoditised.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: High margin value flows to those who own the digital platforms, capture data pipelines and control proprietary algorithms.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If Singapore remains content with being an exceptional adopter of foreign technology, we risk becoming a low margin highway.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The intellectual property and high value decision-making will increasingly sit somewhere else, such as Silicon Valley, Oslo or Shanghai.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To bridge this gap, we must examine our underlying operations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Singapore holds over 200 international shipping groups and thousands of logistics firms, yet day-to-day workflows remain legacy- and relationship-driven.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For many businesses, including our SMEs or other companies operating and managing ships for Singapore, as an example, when a critical machinery anomaly or cargo delays occur at sea, the current process is still highly manual.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The crew logs the issue via email or the vessels' planned maintenance system portal and shore coordinators rely on disconnected spreadsheets or personal networks to solve spare parts and reroute assets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This manual approach persist in many SMEs, even though modern ships generate a vast sea of real-time telemetry sensor data every second.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our national research ecosystem, including agencies, such as the Agency for Science, Technology and Research, can support SMEs in developing and adopting AI-driven predictive maintenance capabilities that analyse real-time operational telemetry to identify abnormal equipment behaviour before failures occur.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such systems could support more efficient spare parts planning, minimise unplanned downtime and strengthen operational reliability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Over time, more intelligent inventory management may also reduce the need for vessels to carry excessive on-board spare part inventories while maintaining safety and resilience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Successive industry transformation maps have pushed for foundational digital standards, sustainable field test beds and basic automated systems.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, our funding philosophies remain too cautious, incremental and focus on short-term software adoption.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While existing support schemes have played an important role in accelerating technology adoption and digitalisation across the sector, a significant proportion of industry expenditure continues to flow towards commercially available solutions developed overseas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Although these technologies can deliver immediate productive gains, they do not necessarily build Singapore-owned intellectual property or create global exportable platforms.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In many cases, we have become successful users of technologies whose long-term economic value ultimately accrues elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To anchor true long-term competitiveness, our funding models can also make a bold shift from subsidising technology adoption to financing proprietary creation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To actively transform Singapore from a world-class transport operator into a global transport architect, I have three suggestions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These programmes can provide deeper co-investment support to consortia comprising of local universities, startup research institutions and transport operators working to develop bigger, globally competitive platforms.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must try to fund homegrown AI-driven global fleet analytics and end-to-end multimodal routing architectures coded and owned here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When international retailers look for global supply chain software, they should buy Singapore-made platforms, ensuring licensing revenues flow back into our economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Two, mandate share data standards via a national transport data trust.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The greatest barrier to developing world-class transport AI is extreme data fragmentation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Every operator guards operational data carefully, often for legitimate commercial reasons.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But this limits the ability of researchers and innovators to train powerful predictive models.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such a clean repository will hopefully attract top global AI talent.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This excellent initiative should expand across our logistics payloads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But we must ensure these rotation programmes include our tech native talent.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should intentionally allocate global rotation lines to local software engineers and data scientists from our transport agencies or companies, deploying them to global tech hubs, like Rotterdam or Silicon Valley.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This will cultivate a specialised hybrid workforce that understands both deep code and ship operations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This extensive focus on platform architecture is fundamentally about safeguarding and upgrading high quality jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Singapore continues to face challenges in maintaining a sufficiently deep pipeline of local Singaporean maritime professionals, particularly in specialised seafaring, engineering and operational roles that underpin our status as a global maritime hub.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For over two decades, the supply of local Singaporean mariners has faced structural pressures as fewer young Singaporeans choose seafaring careers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is difficult to design world-class ship management platforms, train advanced maritime AI systems or lead global maritime enterprises without professionals who possess deep practical experience at sea.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For generations of Singaporean deck officers and marine engineers, it provided a structured pathway to sea experience, rise through the ranks and ultimately, assume command responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The impact was not only felt at sea.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many former NOL officers later transitioned to shore-based roles across ship management, maritime services, logistics, port operations, maritime law and ship finance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The company serves as an important pipeline for the wider maritime ecosystem, including public sector institutions and industry positions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My colleague, the hon MP Kenneth Tiong, will be speaking more on this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Maritime hubs are ultimately built on people and expertise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Ports, vessels and technology can be acquired, but deep operational knowledge and technology takes decades to cultivate.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We therefore need to ensure that Singapore continues to provide sufficient opportunities for our mariners to gain practical sea-going experience and develop into the future leaders of our maritime sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Otherwise, we may one day find ourselves facing an uncomfortable prospect having to look overseas, even for some of the most critical leadership positions, such as our port master, marine superintendents, maritime regulators and industry leaders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: First, the Government must aggressively support and build operational and seafaring careers among Singaporeans to feed our critical onshore management roles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Deep maritime technology is not about replacing our people.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Tan, you have less than a minute to go.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We win by moving ahead of the curve.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Our success has come from connecting people, businesses and ideas with the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: For a small island with no natural resources, connectivity has never simply been about transport.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It has been about survival, resilience and economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: These figures reflect the confidence that global businesses continue to place in Singapore as a trusted gateway to Asia.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But we should never assume this position is guaranteed.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Across our region, countries are investing heavily in ports, airports and logistics infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Technology is reshaping global supply chains, while geopolitical tensions are making trade routes more uncertain.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Businesses today are looking not only for the fastest route, but also for the most reliable and resilient one.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: In this environment, our future competitiveness will depend not only on the infrastructure we build, but also on how intelligently we use it.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: That is why I believe Singapore should focus on three priorities.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: First, we must become the world's smartest transport hub through AI and data.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: For decades, our competitive advantage has been operational excellence.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: The next leap forward will come from intelligence – AI.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: AI can optimise cargo flows, predict equipment failures before they occur, improve vessel and aircraft scheduling and detect supply chain disruptions before they become costly delays.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Imagine identifying a disruption at a regional hub hours before it affects Singapore, allowing shipping schedules to be adjusted automatically, or carrying out maintenance based on predictive analytics rather than fixed schedules, reducing downtime while improving safety.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: They are already being deployed around the world.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It is also working with industry partners to develop AI applications for route optimisation, fuel efficiency and predictive analytics.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: The next step is to connect these efforts across our ports, airports, logistics providers and customs systems into an integrated digital ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: When trusted data flows securely across the supply chain, cargo moves more efficiently, businesses gain greater visibility and resources are used more productively.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, data itself becomes a source of competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Second, Singapore should aspire not only to be a transport hub, but also a transport innovation hub.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Throughout our history, Singapore has succeeded not by inventing every technology ourselves, but by becoming the place where innovations are tested, refined and commercialised.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: We should apply that same philosophy to transport.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Many promising innovations are emerging from SMEs and startups developing AI-powered logistics platforms, autonomous inspection systems, warehouse automation and digital trade solutions.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Our ports and airports should become living test labs where these companies can test their innovations in real operating environments.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: If a Singapore company develops an AI solution that improves cargo handling at Tuas Port or streamlines operations at Changi Airport, that solution can be exported across ASEAN and beyond.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: In doing so, we are not only exporting transport services.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: We are exporting Singaporean innovation, creating new opportunities for our enterprises while strengthening our position in regional value chains.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Third, as technology transforms transport, we must invest just as strongly in our people.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Whenever new technologies emerge, there are understandable concerns about automation replacing jobs.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Technology changes jobs far more often than it eliminates them.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: The real question is whether workers are given the opportunity to adapt.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: As AI becomes embedded across our transport ecosystem, demand will grow for data analysts, systems engineers, cybersecurity specialists and digital operation managers.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It also means helping SMEs adopt new technologies.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Digital transformation should not be something only large multinational companies (MNCs) can afford.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: If our SMEs can access technology, talent and financing, they too can become part of Singapore's next growth story.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Transport today depends on data just as much as it depends on roads, ports and airports.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Cybersecurity, trusted digital identities and secure cross-border data flows are therefore matters of national competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Businesses choose Singapore because they trust our institutions and the reliability of our systems.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: As our transport system becomes increasingly digital, maintaining that trust will become one of our greatest competitive advantages.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Every generation has had to reinvent the foundations of our competitiveness.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Trump's Liberation Day tariffs, Brexit, the success of the far-right in many democratic systems are all reactions to the sense that many across the world have – that globalisation has failed, that we must batten down the hatches to ensure we work toward Singapore – whether me, we or otherwise – first.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, I would argue that this world view risks going down the very same pathways that would further entrench polarisation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Competition and remaining competitive may have been Singapore's lifeblood, but I fear that focusing solely on competitiveness and protection would cause us to leave out areas of growth or potential that we must keep our sights on as we search to find ways and means in which to build a better future for our economy and our country.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It also becomes important to have a hard look at where we stand in a world where truly global supply chains are being unpicked, localised, rewired, where sanctions and trade barriers are being erected and weaponised.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And the role that I believe we must play has to revolve around trust.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Trust that we remain open, predictable and never an instrument of another's strategic goals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And it is also why I believe that our way forward has to be a reframing of the role that we play in the world.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our foreign service teams and Government agencies have done well in promoting and upholding Singapore's role into the international economic order, but more can be done to emphasise Singapore's facilitative approach, that is, to promote Singapore not simply as a competitor but a connector.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should move away from thinking about how we compete with other great ports of the world, how we capture trade flows at the expense of other hubs or to chase that higher ranking on a league table of port throughput, of airport connectivity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should not see our role as accumulating trade flows for ourselves, but instead as a connector for which we make the movement of goods, people, capital and ideas between other parties, smoother, safer, faster and more reliable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Apart from more obvious physical infrastructure, such as roads container ports and airports, we should stay attentive to the growing importance of digital public infrastructure.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is defined generally as foundational hardware, software, regulatory frameworks and networks which allow cross-border exchange of digital ordered or delivered goods and services.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore already has an advantage in this area, particularly in terms of digital intensity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This seems to be borne up by our attempts to digitalise our logistical supply chains.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Way back in 2007, Singapore launched TradeXchange to provide seamless interconnectivity among commercial and regulatory systems for the Singapore trade and logistics community.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In 2018, this was replaced by the Networked Trade Platform.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, this now appears to have been replaced by SGTraDex, the Singapore trade data exchange launched in June 2022.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This platform was backed by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and aims to streamline information flows and promote efficient data sharing across the fragmented global ecosystem through a common data highway.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This new system was launched to facilitate digital trade and deter fraudsters, which became even more pressing in the wake of fraud allegations at trading companies and as demonstrated, itself, as a proof of concept.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, what were the learning points taken on board from the previous attempts and attempted roll-outs of proceeding platforms?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More broadly, Singapore plays an important role in shaping the global digital economy, whether through its network of digital economy agreements or by co-convening the Joint Statement Initiative on E-Commerce at the World Trade Organization.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our agencies deserve commendation for their success in positioning Singapore as a connector despite the highly contested international digital trade landscape.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Nonetheless, as Singapore plays this high-level role, we must look beyond the important but ultimately top-line questions of Singapore's competitiveness in such frameworks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead, we must pay more attention to whether such initiatives actually better the lives of our residents and generate value for our businesses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In particular, we must go beyond helping SMEs digitalise and instead equip them to take advantage of internationalisation in the digital economy so that they are not just moving more effectively digitalising as businesses but evolving to become more valuable in the digital economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That Singapore is seen as relatively weaker in the people pillar of the digital economy could mean that there is room for improvement.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It suggests that Singaporeans and Singaporean companies are benefiting less from the digital economy when compared to those in other economies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must also concern ourselves with the possibility of large MNCs dominating high-value ecosystems while local enterprises take up low-value, low-margin activities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, could the Minister provide more details on our efforts thus far in countering economic enclaving and on our plans to enable SMEs to continue playing their part and building Singapore's role as a connector?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In view of this, we should think carefully about the apparent gap between our Government's efforts, whether domestic or international, and the actual benefits felt by our people and companies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we were recently told that median household market incomes for residents crossed the $12,000 mark, many Singaporeans still worry about wages relative to housing, transport, caregiving and assorted cost of living.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is a sense that even Singaporeans earning decent wages cannot feel secure, particularly when contrasted against job security in an age of AI and digitalisation, and the safety nets available if they are rendered irrelevant by a fast-changing and cut-throat economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our SMEs too, may struggle to see how the high-level agreements signed by our Government have helped them, if the value of any unlocked opportunities are snapped up by larger players and they remain confined to an ever smaller margin.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could the Minister therefore share how the Government assesses whether our digital economy and connectivity strategies are translating into tangible gains for the average Singaporean and Singaporean firms, not only in aggregate data, but in an economy clearly oriented towards better jobs, stronger local enterprises, greater SME participation and a clear pathway for ordinary citizens to benefit from the future phases of growth?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Any discussion about our role in global trade will not be complete without taking into account geopolitical complexities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore needs the free flow of goods, people and data to survive as an island and prosper as a trade-dependent economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This reality makes us susceptible to geopolitical upheavals, major power rivalries and conflicts, even those far beyond our borders and control.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But none of this implies that Singapore cannot and should not do more to mitigate the transportation and connectivity risks we face.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If Singapore's connectivity with the world is disrupted, we will find it hard to make a living, to keep the lights on or even to put food on the table.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Conflicts in Europe and the Middle East have directly affected everyday activity in Singapore, and we continue to feel the consequence today when we pay our utility bills, fill our gas tanks or shop for daily groceries.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Faced with such tumult, we cannot afford to settle for being an oasis of superficial stability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead, we must actively assure both Singaporeans and international partners that Singapore will remain reliable, valuable and connected in any future scenario.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, while the current Government looks at enhancing Singapore's position as a transportation and communications hub, I would like to seek more details on our plans for making Singapore the location of choice, despite our earlier mentioned exposure.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In the plans for transportation, could the Government lay out more fully how they intend to mitigate the risk of Singapore being cut off from global and regional transportation networks and communication lines?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could the Minister clarify the specific risk frameworks and contingency plans that would keep Singapore connected if key maritime, aviation, digital or energy supply routes are disrupted and how these plans and frameworks are coordinated across agencies?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has been severely tested in the past.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic tested resilience of our open economy, bringing to light potential choke points in our access to labour and critical supplies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But today's crises are more complex and fractious, and the coming challenges may be even more wide-ranging and long-lasting.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Deeply integrating contingency planning into the transportation plans at hand will help reassure citizens and partners alike.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, as the world is becoming more volatile and less forgiving, Singapore must redouble efforts to remain globally indispensable and to work to fortify the stable international order on which our prosperity depends.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In doing so, we must champion connection and collaboration instead of close-minded focus on competition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But this larger strategic view must never obscure the real value of economic success.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We do not pursue growth or connectivity for their own sake.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must pay closer attention to whether our policies are really helping our workers, households and businesses feel that our lives are getting better and that we are equipped to face the future economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's development story, the role that we play in connecting the world, has never been just a "once-off" miracle.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In relation to the language in the Motion proposed, I will focus on two points: frontier technologies and good jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I hereby declare my interest as an employee in the aviation sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We are committed to specific green goals, including on carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We are also committed to building a vibrant aviation industry to provide good jobs and continued growth, but we cannot meet both ambitions under the current "business as usual" paradigm.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We need a leap of imagination and technology, a completely new way of doing things.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It is a risky move, but we have made decisive breaks before.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Five decades ago, we made a big bet to move our airport from Paya Lebar to Changi.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We put in place attractive air hub policies, make concerted efforts to grow airlines, airports and ground-handling capabilities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Today, we have a successful and multiple award-winning Changi Airport and SIA.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Changi Airport is now ranked fourth business busiest airport in international passenger traffic and SIA has clinched the world's best airline successively.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Changi Airport is also one of the world's largest air cargo transshipment hub.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This series of successes in our aviation sector are not coincidental.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It took many years of long-term planning, significant investment, systematic development and well-coordinated implementation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The same big leap to create our new and next competitive advantage must begin now.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Our Singaporean psyche of "never rest on our laurels" and "plan for rainy days" will keep us thinking of how do we stay ahead of competition, not just by doing more of what we excel in, but to identify critical weaknesses and develop new competitive advantages.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In key air hubs around the world, there are three constraints limiting growth.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: First, capacity; second, manpower; and third, carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: With the third runway completed and T5 construction underway, the first constraint on capacity growth is being addressed.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The second constraint on manpower is an ongoing challenge.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Many airport staff had left the industry during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We have an ageing population and worsening climate conditions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: To tackle this, we have started concerted R&D innovation efforts in Changi Airport over the past few years, leveraging technology developments in AVs, robotics and AI.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The third constraint in carbon emissions is probably the hardest to crack.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In a recent report published by Transport and Environment, an aviation think tank, Changi Airport is ranked ninth in the world in terms of Scope 3 carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As an expanding air hub, Changi Airport will inevitably chalk up higher carbon emissions so long as aircraft engines continue to burn jet fuel.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In 2024, CAAS released the Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint, the key recommendations included improving the efficiency of air traffic management, increased solar panel deployment in Changi and Seletar airports, expand the use of clean energy around ground vehicles and adopting sustainability aviation fuel by airlines.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Sustainability Aviation Fuel Levy Bill was passed in October 2025 in this House and will take effect from 2027, barring further delays.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The goal is to create certainty in aggregate demand, so as to prime local sustainability aviation fuel production at-scale by key producers, such as Neste.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In 2022, Neste established the world's largest sustainability aviation fuel production facility in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The intent is to start small with 1% to 3% sustainability aviation fuel uplift, because the price of sustainability aviation fuel is currently at least two to five times the cost of normal aviation fuel.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Coupled with the recent war in the Middle East that already drove fuel prices to double their original levels, aviation authorities worldwide will be reluctant to mandate a more aggressive sustainability aviation fuel policy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Moreover, feedstock availability to produce sustainability aviation fuel is limited, so the ability to meet long-term supply capacity at the market competitive cost may still be in question.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Like all fossil fuels, the supply of aviation fuel will one day run out.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In recent years, there are two other streams of technology development for aircraft powered by clean energy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In 2020, Airbus announced the hydrogen powered aircraft concept, ZEROe, for roll-out in 2035.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: However, presumably due to uncertainties of hydrogen as a fuel and the challenges of deploying hydrogen in an operational environment, Airbus has shelved the ZEROe prototype from 2035 by five to 10 years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Meanwhile, another track to design and manufacture battery-operated hybrid-electric and electric aircraft has been progressing steadily.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: With the rapid improvements in battery technology, it is estimated that in 15 years' time, hybrid-electric aircraft flights for short-haul flights within a range of 1,000 nautical miles will become a reality.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: From Singapore, popular destinations within a 1,000 nautical mile radius include Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta, Phuket, Langkawi, Medan and Tioman.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Worldwide, about half of flights operated are short-haul flights under three-hour flight times and up to 1,000 nautical mile range.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As battery technology developments have been making rapid progress, hybrid-electric and eventually, fully electric aircraft could replace conventional aircraft for these routes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is a game changer in carbon emissions reduction, and we must spot the trend and the technology early.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: If we can do so and establish ourselves as an international green air hub, that will not only address our growing carbon emissions challenge, but also cement our position in sustainable aviation and in turn, create many new opportunities for Singapore's aviation and aerospace industry.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We have done this before for new technologies in the past.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: For example, the Economic Development Board (EDB) brought in Hyundai Motors Group to set up its electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing plants in Singapore, even though we did not have any car manufacturing track record and facilities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This approach is how Toulouse became the home of Airbus and Seattle became the home of Boeing decades ago.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: However, with trillions of dollars worth of back orders, neither of these two hubs are focused on becoming hubs of the future aircraft.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We are an established international aviation and aerospace hub, with a mature and thriving ecosystem of aviation, original equipment manufacturer (OEMs), MRO facilities, IHLs training aerospace engineers and technicians, 80 airlines, three runways and we will have five terminals and a new aviation industrial zone.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We have a biennial Singapore Airshow and a very pro-innovation, pro-investment funding and financing environment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Moreover, Singapore sits in the centre of the world's fastest growing region for aviation, comprising India, China and Southeast Asia.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The carbon emissions in the supply chain logistics in terms of aircraft manufacturing, assembly testing and delivery would be minimised.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There is a famous saying by a Chinese philosopher, Mencius: "To achieve success, the right timing, right place and right people must coexist." Now is the time, Singapore is the place, what is needed to turn us into an international green air hub is the right partners who share this ambition and are willing to work together to realise this vision.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Our Singapore is already home to the regional headquarters of conventional aircraft manufacturers, Boeing and Airbus, smaller aircraft manufacturers, such as Embraer and Avions de Transport Régional, and new players in the electric aircraft space, such as Elysian Aircraft, Heart Aerospace, Nimbus Aviation, Electra and Mitsubishi Aircraft Corporation, are mostly based in the Western world in North America and Europe.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Similar to how the Chinese EV manufacturers are disrupting the automobile industry, this electric aircraft companies will be the new darlings shaping the future of the aviation industry.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The first step is to attract this disruptors, electric aircraft manufacturers to set up base in Singapore for R&D.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Next is to connect them with funding platforms, such as the National Research Foundation (NRF) and EDB, as well as the private and institutional investors and banking sector financiers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: And finally, to connect the electric aircraft manufacturers with their potential customers, namely major airlines operating short-haul routes in the region, such as SIA, Scoot, Lion Air, AirAsia Group and VietJet.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The value we bring as an established international air hub to these electric aircraft manufacturers is invaluable, because they can immediately plug into a robust and ready machinery, and fulfil fast-growing aggregated demand, financed by low-cost and abundant funding.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The aircraft manufacturers can stay focused on their niche expertise and bring product to market in the shortest time.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: An international green air hub does not just benefit the aviation industry.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We will be an R&D Centre of Excellence for the IHLs and young aerospace engineers for the long term.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Currently, the National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University both offer undergraduate courses in aerospace engineering.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Graduates may join MRO companies like ST Aerospace or aircraft engine companies like Rolls Royce, but doing mostly maintenance work.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: One of my young residents, N, 18 years old, is an aspiring final year student at Ngee Ann Polytechnic, studying aerospace engineering.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: She is mulling over whether she should continue to pursue a university degree in aerospace engineering or a more traditional engineering degree in mechanical engineering.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: She shared that if there are more exciting R&D opportunities in aerospace, like designing and manufacturing an aircraft, her decision would have been very clear.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Young Singaporeans want to be challenged and we can create opportunities for them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We can also attract world-class talents in aerospace engineering to work and live here.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In time, Singaporean engineers and designers can become world-class leaders in this nascent field.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They can apply the latest AI and 3D printing technologies to design and build an electric aircraft from scratch.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Moreover, many young people very much care about the environment and want to contribute to the decarbonisation journey.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This will be a new engine of growth.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is the use of frontier technologies to secure good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is the story of the past, which has given us our prosperity and our place in this world today and this can be the story of our future – and we must take to the skies and reshape our destiny once again.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Our major gateways like Changi Airport and the Port of Singapore have enabled our nation to punch above our weight.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Our future success will rely on us being at the forefront of connecting people, markets, ideas and capital.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Today's Motion affirms the role of a world-class infrastructure in reinforcing Singapore's position as a global transport hub and anchoring good jobs in, Singapore.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: All of us here can appreciate how and why this is important.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, I hope the House will join me in reflecting whether our world-class infrastructure should only have the purposes of consolidating our status as a transport hub and anchoring jobs here.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Should we not ponder on the question who should our world-class infrastructure serve?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Should our class infrastructure merely facilitate the movement of capital, goods and talent across borders?
