speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Or should it also improve and enhance the everyday lives of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My answer, Mr Speaker, is that our world-class infrastructure should not just create economic opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, it is also imperative that our class infrastructure is something that serves our citizens directly.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As far as possible, our infrastructure should not merely facilitate Singaporeans getting good jobs but also tangibly improve the lived experiences of our people.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: By this, I mean ensuring that Singaporeans can genuinely enjoy or benefit from our infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Changi Airport offers an example of what I mean.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It is also well loved by Singaporeans, something that we all are proud of.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Even if one is not catching a flight, one can spend an afternoon at Jewel.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Families can gather there for meal at one of the many wonderful restaurants.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Couples can go for a date at the Canopy Park and everyone, young and old, can enjoy the Rain Vortex.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Changi Airport is an excellent model of infrastructure that generates economic value while simultaneously enriching the everyday lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Yes, the airport creates job opportunities but it also offers social and recreational amenities to ordinary Singaporeans, including those who are not frequent flyers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And I think it is good that Changi Airport is not merely the preserve of jetsetting elite but open to all Singaporeans in the sense that there will always be something for someone to do that even if they are not catching a flight.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In our pursuit to be a globally connected aviation, maritime and logistics hub, we must ensure that Singaporeans are not and do not feel alienated from the world-class infrastructure which underpins and makes possible the hub status.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Allow me to further illustrate my point with the more mundane example of expressways.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Goods can be efficiently transported from our port terminals to our industrial estates and commercial zones and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: But while we appreciate the economic efficiencies created by our network of expressways, we should also keep in mind that two-thirds of Singaporean resident households that do not own cars, including myself.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These two examples of our airport and our expressways hopefully clarify my point that our infrastructure should be designed with public access in mind.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: There are, however, peak hour restrictions on weekday mornings for holders of the older persons' Freedom Pass.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: There is a study on the Freedom Pass, which was published in 2014, and I hope to read part of the abstract into the record.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In their article, "More than A to B: the role of free bus travel for the mobility and well-being of older citizens in London", the author stated that "travelling by bus provided opportunities for meaningful social interaction.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Travelling as art of the 'general public' provided a sense of belonging and visibility in the public arena, a socially acceptable way of tackling chronic loneliness.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Crucially, it makes senior citizens feel like they belong and have a place in society.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This comes back to my earlier point that Singaporeans must not feel alienated from our world-class infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans, regardless of age or means, must be able to use that infrastructure, not merely benefit economically from them.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I should acknowledge that my hon friend from Sengkang, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, had also called for off-peak public transport to be made free for seniors and persons with disabilities during the 14th Parliament.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The then Minister for Transport, S Iswaran, rebuffed this proposal with the warning that the ensuing financial burden is by no means insignificant.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The WP has consistently argued that public transport should be viewed primarily as a public service rather than a profit centre.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Especially for our seniors, public transport helps to fulfil important non-material needs such as for companionship, community and belonging.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These are sometimes overlooked when we consider the matter only in terms of dollars and cents.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As Singapore becomes a super-aged society, I believe that our senior citizens here similarly deserve their own Merdeka Pass.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While AI threatens to change the face of many professions, we continue to face persistent labour shortages in the public transportation sector.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Acting Minister for Transport has also acknowledged that recruitment and retention are the biggest challenges preventing further expansion of the bus network.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Frontier technologies, like AVs, could offer a potential solution.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We could start by running self-driving night buses along existing Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) lines when these lines are closed during the overnight hours.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Late night bus services have in the past suffer from low ridership and the NightRider and Nite Owl Services have been discontinued since the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: But even before the pandemic, we never had a proper network of late bus services that replicate even on a limited basis the connectivity provided during daylight hours, unlike in other major global cities like London, New York, Hong Kong or Beijing.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The pre-pandemic NightRider and Nite Owl services only operated uni-directionally, from the city to various housing estates, and primarily serviced people having a night out in the city.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: But a proper network of self-driving late night buses bus services, running along existing MRT lines would be truly revolutionary for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It would not just benefit Singaporeans enjoying the nightlife, but also people who finish or start work after the MRT shuts down, and staff and travellers going to the airport for late night flights.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Affordable late-night mobility should be part of a vibrant, world city like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Eventually, we can even consider expanding AVs to support school bus services, which is another area where a shortage of drivers and rising cost pressures have made it more difficult for school bus operators to sustain operations.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For example, AVs could be used to shuttle students who live more than four kilometres from their school since bus operators are now no longer contractually required serve them.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is not to suggest that automation is a substitute for valuing human work.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Even with AVs, Singaporeans will continue to depend on thousands of bus captains for the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While we rely on AVs to supplement our manpower needs, we must continue to make sure that our bus operators enjoy the wages, career progression and working conditions that commensurate with the skills and socially valuable work that they do.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Bus driving should be seen as a profession Singaporeans should be proud to enter and not simply one that we struggle to fulfil.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As we have seen with Changi Airport, Singapore is capable of building infrastructure that both impresses the world and benefits the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Changi drives our economic competitiveness while simultaneously being a place for Singaporeans to gather, relax, celebrate and create memories.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: So, as we develop the infrastructure befitting a global hub status, I hope the House can appreciate that the real measure of a truly world-class infrastructure is whether the people who build our country can truly enjoy it.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Before I proceed, I would like to declare my interest as the chief executive officer of Strides Premier, a subsidiary of SMRT.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As someone who has been in the transport sector for years, I have watched this space very closely.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Almost 10 years ago, I took my very first AV ride with nuTonomy at One-North.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It was groundbreaking for its time, but looking back, it was quite basic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If there was a simple obstacle on the road, the vehicle came to a dead halt, it could not even overtake.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Fast forward to the last couple of years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I have personally tested Waymo in the US, Mobileye in Germany, Baidu Apollo Go, WeRide and Pony.ai in China.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They are fully mature robotaxis taking fare-paying passengers, navigating complex mega-cities daily.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Meanwhile, here at home, we are also conducting localised AV trials in Punggol.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But the critical question is: are our people ready?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: To understand what is at stake, we must look at the human face of the point-to-point (P2P) transport sector.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In 2013, before the explosion of private hire cars (PHCs), Singapore had over 28,000 taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For many of them, driving is a job of the last resort.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is the safety net that keeps their families afloat, bringing home an average of about $3,000 a month.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many have opted this line of job due to changes in industries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Driving taxis or PHCs, for some, is the job of last resort to maintain an average salary.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If AVs were to replace just 10% of this fleet, displacing 7,000 drivers, where will they go?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It will be an uphill battle for Singapore to find equivalent jobs with similar pay for 7,000 of our fellow citizens.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Not all of them will be able to adapt to new jobs associated with our new AI-led economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We cannot afford to let them become the collateral damage of progress.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Therefore, I would like to urge MOT and our tripartite partners to take a proactive, human-centric approach to this transition.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I suggest a clear, strategic framework to deal with this situation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First, we need to strategically deploy AVs to areas that are currently underserved by our pool of P2P drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Every day, passengers struggle to find rides to remote industrial areas like Tuas and Jurong Island, and to some extend, leisure spots like Sentosa and Mandai Wildlife Reserve – because drivers are reluctant to go there due to the low chance of finding a return passenger.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Similarly, finding a ride in the wee hours of the morning remains a challenge for many commuters.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Let us consider deploying AVs to plug these exact operational gaps and serve the underserved, rather than pitting machines against our drivers in high-demand zones.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, we must look at retraining with a dose of realism.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I urge MOT to collaborate with the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) or the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) to convert some of our displaced P2P drivers into controllers at AV operations control centres to monitor fleets and to take over the AVs during unusual circumstances and during emergencies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, we need to be brutally honest with ourselves.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As each controller is expected to oversee up to 15 AVs concurrently, the math simply does not add up.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: There will not be enough controller jobs for every displaced driver.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Furthermore, these roles require entirely new tech skill sets that some existing drivers may not possess.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Therefore, MOT and NTUC need to work aggressively with various agencies, including the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and social service sectors to provide comprehensive Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We need to look beyond land transport and transition these drivers into other structural growth sectors of our economy, such as healthcare, or our booming aviation sector, including the upcoming new T5.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is highly unlikely that AVs will displace a massive number of P2P drivers in the near term, but we must start planning today, so that our people will be prepared.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: While we have to move cautiously on robotaxis to ensure safety and because of the direct impact on Singaporean livelihoods, we should do the exact opposite where we face severe domestic shortages.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must deploy AVs where we have a high reliance on foreign labour.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: LTA recently had to work with Public Transport Operators to significantly increase the starting pays and sign-on bonuses for bus captains.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In 2021, Singaporeans and Permanent Residents made up 54% of our bus captains.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Assuming they are completely safe, autonomous buses are the exact solution we need to mitigate this acute domestic manpower crunch.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: LTA is already trialing AVs for bus services 400 and 91, but we can consider doing more.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I urge MOT to consider investing more capital, pouring in more resources and moving with a much greater sense of urgency.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The same logic applies to our maritime and aviation sectors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These critical economic engines have a heavy, structural reliance on foreign labour where deep automation would be immensely valuable.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, unlike robotaxis, AV deployment in these heavy industrial sectors yields lower immediate commercial returns, making private players hesitant to shoulder the massive upfront risk alone.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: MOT and the related agencies could intervene, co-invest and accelerate adoption by making far better use of the NRF's funding under the RIE2030 framework.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Instead of small, isolated pilots, we need to direct these national resources toward high-impact, scaled-up industrial applications.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: By boldly backing these strategic sectors, we can solve our structural labour constraints while firmly securing Singapore's position as a premier, future-ready global transport hub.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: (In Mandarin):   In early June this year, at the invitation of LTA, I brought nearly 50 residents and grassroots leaders to Punggol to personally experience a ride in the AVs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Although a safety driver was present onboard, residents could see it clearly for themselves that the steering wheel in the AV was turning on its own.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Throughout the entire 20-minute journey, there was no need for any human intervention whatsoever.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When obstacles appeared on the road, the self-driving car navigated around them with ease and continued on its way.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: One resident remarked with wonder: "With my eyes closed, I wouldn't have known I was in a self-driving car at all." I smiled and asked: "If there were no safety driver in the AV, would you still dare to ride in it?" Another resident immediately replied: "I'd want to even more – because without a driver around, you'd have more privacy!" The positive response from residents surprised me somewhat.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Everyone marvelled that self-driving cars were no longer a scene in a science fiction movie, but a reality right before our eyes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Yet even as people were excited about the technology, a moment of silence fell and residents, almost in unison, gave voice to a deep and shared concern: what will become of our taxi drivers and ride-hailing drivers in the future?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For them, ferrying passengers is the safety net that keeps their entire families fed, housed, and clothed.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: While AVs may not pose too great a disruption to them in the near term, we must plan ahead.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We cannot wait until the rain has soaked us through before thinking to find shelter.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We cannot allow these drivers who have quietly served Singapore all these years to become casualties of technological progress.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: On the contrary, we must help them through the transition and make them a vital new force across our emerging industries. : Mr Speaker, Sir, disruption is inevitable, but hardship for our workers is not.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Innovation is a tool, but compassion must be our guide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Let us prepare Singapore for the AV revolution, not by rushing to replace our local drivers, but by strategically using technology to solve our deepest manpower deficits, while protecting, retraining and honouring the human beings who keep our nation moving every single day.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is a maritime nation in the fullest sense – the world's busiest container transhipment port, the world's largest bunkering hub, and by one global ranking, the leading maritime city on the planet.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The sea is not one sector among many for us; it is the foundation we were built on.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We are an island that imports more than nine in 10 of our calories across the water and we sit astride the Straits of Malacca, through which roughly a quarter of all seaborne trade and nearly half the world's seaborne crude oil moves.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A nation this dependent on the sea cannot safely treat the capability to move on it as a commodity to be rented.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Yet, over two decades, we quietly gave away one of its core sovereign capabilities – a shipping line of our own.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In so doing, we exited an entire strategic domain.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We did this right as every serious maritime nation moved the other way.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: China built COSCO into an arm of national power.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Even Australia, down to a dozen trading ships, is legislating a national strategic fleet.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They are states that understand shipping is a strategic capability, not a commodity service to be rented.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And our own Government knows this – in the air! "For Changi to work well and succeed", it told this House, "You must first have an anchor national carrier – SIA".

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When SIA neared collapse, Temasek put in up to $15 billion dollars to keep it alive.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We treat the airline, SIA, as strategic and rescue it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But we treat the sea carrier, NOL, as a commodity and sell it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Temasek has since bought into a different carrier – Pacific International Lines (PIL) – but we hold it for a return, not for a purpose.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, Singapore stands as a major maritime hub with no national line of its own.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It sold NOL on the argument that container shipping is fungible.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The box does not care whose ship it rides in.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It does not defend SIA on those grounds at all.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It keeps the airline because a national carrier is a strategic asset in its own right: a capability the country controls, the people it trains and the option to direct it in a crisis.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Government has not stopped believing a national carrier is strategic – it has only stopped believing it for the sea.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The case for selling NOL rested on a category error: that a shipping line is just freight and freight is fungible.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A national line is two strategic capabilities bound together.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, it is the academy that makes our maritime people.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is a ladder that runs from the deck of the ship to the command of a port, and every rung is built on the one below.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A cadet stands his watches and qualifies as an officer of the watch, then as shift mate and, a decade or more on, as master.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The engine room climbs the same way to the chief engineer.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: None of this can be done in a classroom or bought with a grant because each certificate is a legal product of documented sea time on a working ship.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That sea time is the entry ticket for the shore roles that keep the port's waters safe.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The harbour pilot who boards and berths the largest ships afloat, and the surveyors who inspect them must, by the rules, hold those certificates.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And above them sits the Port Master, the statutory officer who can order any vessel in our waters to move, stop or stay.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's Port Masters have been a line of master mariners – Captain M Segar, who came up as a cadet and a harbour pilot, then port master, then rose to assistant chief executive of MPA; and Captain Lee Cheng Wee, the harbour pilot in the early 1970s whom the Government held up in this year's Budget debate as an example for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: No one is being made a master mariner by a scholarship.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Marine command is the one part of the port that still requires a master's ticket – and we are failing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our cadets must seek their sea time on foreign ships and may face a lack of access.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Britain watched its officer corps age and shrink as its fleet flagged out and then had to pay shipowners, through the tax code, to train cadets again.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Australia, down from 100 trading ships to about a dozen, is now legislating a strategic fleet to rebuild the skills they had lost.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Ships can be bought or chartered within a year, but a generation of sea-experienced Singaporeans takes a generation to grow.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When Temasek sold NOL, it crystallised a financial gain – a one-time figure on a balance sheet – and sold the entire training ground which the whole ladder stands on.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Cut the feet away at the foot of the ladder and a decade or more on, the top of it empties.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We have been in search of lost time ever since.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In the long run, the seafaring core of our own port, our harbour pilots and the marine command above them, cannot be kept Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It must be staffed, like our own flag already is, by other nations' officers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second is directable capacity – the difference between sovereignty and dependence in a crisis.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Container space is rationed whenever effective capacity is squeezed faster than it can be replaced.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The demand surged at the pandemic, when rates rose seven-fold, or risk-driven diversions, like the Red Sea, where rerouting every ship around Africa swallowed a-tenth of the world's capacity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In such a crunch, the market does not serve all comers equally.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The carriers still sailing gave priority to exporters under their own flag.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Korea ordered HMM to ringfence space for Korean firms.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A nation relying on foreign lines is served last, at whatever price is named.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A country that owns no capacity in a capacity crunch is a beggar for allocation and will be served with all others.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I put this to the Government in April.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Its answer was that our supply lines are secured by diversification, our standing as a trusted hub and a wide network of global shipping lines.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I respectfully disagree and I think it conflates the role of the port and the carrier.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It turns on the ambiguity in the word "node".

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When we call ourselves a node, we mean "leverage" – some power to bend the flow of trade our way.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But a hub port only gives you half of that.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It gives you centrality – the power to attract.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But it does not give you leverage – the power to make ships that call, serve us first when it counts or to train our merchant navy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: After all, a neutral hub holds its traffic only by staying competitive.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Even winning that competition, if it wins, is not the same as holding leverage.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The carrier picks its port, but the port cannot pick its carriers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When space runs short, it is the carrier that rations it, not the port.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The sale of NOL and the stripping before it, were Temasek's calls.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The same Temasek that in 2020 put $15 billion dollars into rescuing SIA.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I am asking the Government to treat sovereign shipping as what it is – a strategic capability to be rebuilt deliberately.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we wanted to rebuild a national carrier, we would not start from zero.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But Heliconia currently holds it the way it holds any company, as an investment for a return.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It calls itself, in its own words, an SME-enabler.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: PIL is run as a profit-maximising line by a professional chief executive under no national duty of any kind, no obligation to reserve capacity for Singapore in a crisis, no Singaporean crew requirement even on the ships that fly our flag, no training quota and the one voluntary scheme it has is winding down – and no mandatory routes that it must run.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: PIL could be given a national mandate, held both for a return and also to train our officers, to hold capacity that can be directed when a crisis comes and backed to grow over time.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: PIL's moat is a niche – Africa and the global South.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is not fully the academy that we need because our port is an East-West machine – Asia, Europe and transpacific arteries, the largest ships afloat and transshipment at scale that only those lanes generate.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, the real questions are how much of the East-West capability that we gave up with NOL we now have to rebuild and how far up the ladder we are willing to climb to do it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At the floor, a national mandate over PIL as it stands, a training quota, reserved crisis capacity, a Singaporean crew requirement on the ships that fly our flag for a cost of about tens of millions a year.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The next rung, back PIL to climb into the East-West trades.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At first, through slot charters and vessel sharing, rebuilding the operational skills our hub actually runs on.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At the top, owning mainline tonnage outright, the capital-heavy commitment a serious rebuild demands.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Each rung costs more and buys more sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But standing still is also a choice and the one that ends in the port unable to crew its own senior ranks.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Korea's Korea Ocean Business Corporation is a statutory body charged by law with maintaining an essential national shipping system, financing the fleet and guaranteeing tonnage.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We, too, should also consider a binding obligation to train our Singaporean cadets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And to be clear about the costs, scale in the mainline trades is brutal and capital hungry, which is why it needs to be Government-backed, phased and built with patience.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we were to do it, it would cost us billions, too.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But to balk at that cost means having almost no Singaporean sailors manning Singapore's ports.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, we need to decide if we are going to create a system to perpetuate Singaporeans in our own maritime industry and ports, to rebuild our own leverage over shipping capacity – whether we are a country that means to own a ship or one content to crew someone else's.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Or if we want to be a country that does not have the ships to train our own people in ship-faring and that will, in the next supply shock, stand as a price taker in its own port.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: One, by the same logic that makes SIA the anchor in the air, why does a national carrier stops mattering at the water's edge?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Two, if we mean to grow our own seafarers, how do we make a master mariner with no fleet to make him or her on?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And who then fills a marine command our own port depends on?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I rise in support of the Motion tabled by my fellow MOT GPC colleagues.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Over the past few months, the GPC has engaged extensively with industry leaders and experts because we believe this is the right time to take a strategic relook of transport in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While we continue improving our transport system for the daily needs of Singaporeans, we must also recognise transport as a cornerstone of Singapore's long-term economic competitiveness in an increasingly fragmented and uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This Motion is, therefore, about far more than transport.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our position as a leading aviation, maritime and logistics hub was never inevitable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It was earned through decades of bold leadership, long-term planning and the discipline to stay ahead of change.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Around us, countries are building bigger airports, deeper ports and larger logistics parks.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singapore must create new sources of competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I will shape the framework through four interconnected ideas: first, strengthen Singapore's international leadership by shaping global standards and leading aviation and maritime governance; second, build an integrated regional transport and manufacturing ecosystem that deepens connectivity and multiplies ASEAN's collective competitiveness; third, harness frontier technologies and AI to transform Singapore from a trusted transport hub into the trusted orchestrator of intelligent, multimodal transport and logistics flows; and finally, treat transport not merely as infrastructure but as a national economic strategy that creates new engines of growth, high-value jobs and long-term prosperity for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singapore's success has never been built on geography alone.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Every aircraft departing Changi depends not only on our airport, but on international agreements that allow aircraft to move safely across borders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Every vessel entering our ports depends on trusted institutions, common standards and international cooperation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The recent Singapore-Indonesia Flight Information Region agreement, together with disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, reminds us that diplomacy, trusted partnerships and international law remain strategic assets.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As countries invest in bigger infrastructure, Singapore cannot compete on size alone.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must compete by shaping the rules that govern global transport.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: History shows that countries which write tomorrow's rules rarely struggle to compete under them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While we continue to strength institutions, at the same time, Singapore should lead the governance of next-generation transport from low-level airspace management systems (LLAMSs), cross-border drone corridors and autonomous aviation to AI-enabled air traffic management, autonomous vessels and digital maritime standards.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Unlike today's conventional air traffic control, an LLAMS would safely integrate drones, autonomous cargo aircraft and future urban air mobility through dynamic routing, digital flight authorisation, geofencing, AI traffic optimisation and real-time conflict management.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This would create the regulatory and digital foundation for regional drone corridors, further linking Singapore with the region, and unlocking new opportunities in industrial logistics, offshore energy, maritime inspection and autonomous cross-border services.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: To create value, we must build a larger ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Which brings me to my second point on building the ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If international leadership gives us influence, regional integration gives us scale.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We often view aviation, maritime and land transport as separate sectors.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, our future advantage will not come from having the best airport or the best port in isolation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It will come from orchestrating them as one intelligent regional ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The development of Changi Airport T5 presents a once-in-a-generation opportunity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But the greater opportunity lies beyond just connectivity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Imagine advanced manufacturing systems manufactured in Changi, with its semiconductor chips leaving Pasir Ris, with AI-enabled fleet management and autonomous software developed in the Punggol Digital District, with logistics coordinated from our Tampines Logistics Hub, financing arranged in the central business district and supporting products coming from the Johor Special Economic Zone and BBK free trade zone reaching out to global markets – all operating as one intelligent economic system.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That is the ecosystem that we should build.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Few countries possess such a dense concentration of aerospace, advanced manufacturing, logistics, digital industries and transport infrastructure within such a compact footprint.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our ambition should not be to compete with our neighbours, but to multiply this region's collective strengths.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singapore can anchor advanced manufacturing, aerospace engineering, R&D, financing and supply chain orchestration, while complementary manufacturing takes place where land, labour and natural resources are more competitive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singapore can become the world's trusted hub for battery certification, financing, commodity trading, sustainability assurance and global logistics.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Transport can no longer create prosperity simply by moving goods.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Regional integration gives us scale, but scale alone will not define the future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Which brings me to my third point, on leading with frontier technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singapore should establish itself as a global centre of excellence for AI-enabled multimodal transport, logistics and industrial optimisation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: To realise this vision, I would like to propose three national initiatives.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Rather than optimising individual companies as part of a value chain, it would be using agentic AI and integrating maritime, both high-altitude and low-altitude, and land digital twins to orchestrate cargo seamlessly across ports, airports, drone corridors, roads, warehouses and customs as one intelligent national network.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By integrating AVs, drones, harbour craft and intelligent logistics systems under a common national regulatory framework, Singapore can pioneer regional drone corridors and autonomous freight networks that become the global reference model for future logistics.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It will belong to those with the smartest transport ecosystems.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singapore already has the trust, connectivity and talent.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must now invest more boldly in research, innovation and enterprise so that we do not simply participate in the future of global transport.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We often think of transport as just a sector.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I believe we should think of it as an enabler of our economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Every investment in transport multiplies opportunities across every other sector.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It strengthens advanced manufacturing, anchors global supply chains, accelerates the digital economy, attracts investment and creates better jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As supply chains become increasingly shaped by AI, data and geopolitical changes, the countries that create the greatest value will not necessarily manufacture everything themselves.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They will design, coordinate and optimise how the entire network operates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I am especially pleased that Pasir Ris-Changi will host the OneAviation Career Fair later this month, creating opportunities for more Singaporeans to participate in this exciting future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Because ultimately, our greatest competitive advantage will never be our infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our future depends on our ability to lead, connect the region and harness smart technologies to drive the economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Transport is not just about building roads, MRT lines, ports or airports.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must take the lead in shaping international standards, strengthening partnerships with our neighbours and harnessing AI to position Singapore as the regional hub for smart transport and logistics coordination.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our goal is not to compete with our neighbours, but to build a stronger and more prosperous ASEAN together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If Singapore was once known as a global transport hub, we must now aim even higher to become the "orchestra of ASEAN transport for the world", that coordinates the movement of goods, capital, technology, ideas and talent across the region.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By doing so, we can create more high-value jobs, attract quality investments and secure lasting prosperity for all Singaporeans. : Mr Speaker, allow me to conclude with a simple framework.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: O, we orchestrate with AI and frontier technologies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And W, we win by creating greater economic value, better jobs and better lives for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For the past 60 years, Singapore mastered the movement of ships.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Today, we are mastering the movement of data.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is to orchestrate the movement of everything else – of people, goods, capital, ideas, technology, opportunity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That is the difference between being a transport hub and becoming the operating system of Asia's economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we succeed, Singapore will not simply connect the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And that is why I stand in whole-hearted support of this Motion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government's traditional playbook focuses heavily on building world-class infrastructure like Changi Airport T5 and the Tuas next-generation port.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, focusing too much on physical infrastructure carries structural risks in a changing global economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If we do not own the shipping lines or control the underlying cargo movements, relying solely on massive, physical infrastructure leaves our economy exposed to a sunk-cost dependency risk.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The global trading system is under threat from protectionism and geopolitical rivalries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In addition, there is a possibility that an opening of the Northern Sea route through the Arctic or the creation of a land bridge across or a canal through the Kra Isthmus will divert maritime traffic away from Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The massive fixed cost of our expanded port may become a fiscal drag if shipping volumes fall short of the Government's projections, The long-term justification for Changi T5's massive capacity relies on historical hub and spoke models where long-distance traffic requires consolidated transit nodes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, next-generation hyper-efficient aircraft, such as a long-range narrow body Airbus A321XLR, completely disrupts this model.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This aircraft allows airlines to establish economically viable, long and thin direct routes between secondary cities without requiring physical stopovers or refuelling hubs like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a result, Changi Airport may face the risk of capital expansions outpacing the growth of traditional transit passengers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To hedge our exposure to physical trade volatility, Singapore must pivot from being just a physical gatekeeper to also becoming the sovereign digital architect of global trade.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By anchoring the financial, legal and operational code of international shipping lines within Singapore's data jurisdiction, we secure a stronger position of leverage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even if mega alliances berth physically at regional competitors ports, the critical financial transaction layers and supply chain networks running those operations will still run through digital nodes owned by Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must therefore rebalance our long-term capital spending.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As my hon friend, the MP of Hougang, Dennis Tan, highlighted, Singapore must shift from being an outstanding adopter of foreign technology to a creator of our own proprietary systems if we want to capture high margin value.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By securing direct ownership over these foundational digital assets across international trading jurisdictions, we can protect our economic independence and collect licensing rents globally.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This allows us to successfully reduce our reliance on absolute volatile physical cargo throughput, ensuring our national revenue is buffered even if global trade patterns shift away from our shores.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We do not just need a more competitive hub.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need a structurally resilient one that owns the software of global trade, rather than just the concrete that sits on it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This strategic resilience must also extend to the second pillar of the Motion, which champions the use of frontier technologies to anchor good jobs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While automation drives corporate efficiency, we must build a system that governs these tools to protect the daily working conditions of our workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If we do not actively govern the code running inside of our transport infrastructure, frontier technology can inadvertently lead to the extraction of productivity solely at the expense of human well-being.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The report notes that competitive pressures related to cost efficiency and timely deliveries have driven an increased centralisation of control and monitoring through corporate governance structures, shifting the power balance within organisations heavily towards management.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In advanced logistics networks across the world, we are already witnessing these technologies being used in ways that constrain worker autonomy and intensify the pace of work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For instance, the report highlights automated postal and distribution networks, where algorithms generate precise hyper-optimised itineraries, giving workers compressed exact time slots for each delivery.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These machine-generated instructions can become so detailed that they leave minimal space for human judgement or physical adjustments.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The report also underscores cases of asymmetric accountability and glitch penalisation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Workers are uniquely vulnerable to connectivity issues and system failures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a result, workers risk being unfairly held accountable for mistakes originating from computer errors rather than human errors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The report found that the introduction of digital tools had a positive impact on job quality in some more developed countries but a negative impact in some developing ones.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The authors attributed this to differences in institutional and regulatory frameworks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Businesses in Singapore have to use digital tools to improve productivity and efficiency, but we must also ensure that these changes will benefit workers rather than harm them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our goal should not be to ban automation or to turn our backs on technology, but to govern it so that productivity gains are equitably shared with workers rather than extracted solely from their physical and mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To achieve this, I wish to make three policy proposals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will give terminal safety supervisors and operations managers the clear statutory authority to adjust AI targets via safety buffer during peak operational strain or adverse weather without incurring penalties.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Any automated tracking platform used to grade performance, allocate split shifts or determine contract renewals must provide employees with a clear, plain language breakdown of its underlying metrics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This ensures workers have open accessible administrative channels to contest unfair automated penalties caused by network disruptions, hardware glitches or system errors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When transport logistics and aviation operators which achieve major productivity breakthrough through the use of AI, those productivity gains must be shared.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must instead make it our goal to ensure that as our infrastructure and machines grow more capable, our citizens grow more secure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By implementing these targeted worker safeguards and digital asset strategies, we can ensure that technological progress serves the dignity, economic agency and long-term resilience of every Singaporean.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In logistics, new, higher-paying roles will be created in professional, manager and executive (PME) jobs, including data analysis, supply chain management and software development.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, some roles will undergo displacement, including operators, storekeepers and in sales and customer services functions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At our container terminals at Tuas, Pasir Panjang and cargo terminals at Jurong Port, usage of more automated vehicles and cranes will likely and very much improve productivity and create more higher value jobs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we build this future, we must also ask – how are we preparing our people for it?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What struck me was how rapidly technology is changing transport systems around the world.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Across countries and industries, there is a growing push towards automation, digitalisation and new operating models.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The lesson I took away was that it reinforced the need for Singapore to continue adapting, innovating and investing in our people if we are to maintain our position as a leading global transportation hub.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But it is our workers – their skills, their adaptability and professionalism – that will continue to differentiate Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And that brings us back to the central question: how are we preparing Singaporeans for this future?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my roles as a labour MP and in my work in M3+ under Focus Area Four (FA4) where we look into employment and employability, the question that many Singaporean workers are most concerned about is: will I have a good job in Singapore’s future?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, when we adopt more automation, robotics and AI in our transport sector, let us also ask: how can these technologies help create better jobs for our seafarers, our technicians, our aviation, logistics and maritime workers, and new roles in transport cybersecurity as our sectors become more digitalised?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As our rail network expands, with projects like the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link, how can we create ladders to help our rail technicians progress further?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And as we develop the low-altitude economy, including deploying more drones and also unmanned vessels for surveys, how are we creating more career pathways for Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The future of transport must also be a future of career progression, where our workers have the opportunities to become more skilled, more productive, with better wages and better work prospects than before.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, today, I would like to speak on how we can create a better future for our young graduates and our existing rank-and-file workers and technicians.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my work as an educator, I have watched many of my young students drawn to delivery and gig work to pass time, for their flexibility, and probably the chance to earn slightly extra income.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I understand the appeal, but the job has its downsides.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, there is also limitation in their progression in the long run.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our young delivery riders risk becoming entrenched in these jobs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And there are signs of potential disruptions too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, as we anchor good jobs through the development of our transport industries, we must also adjust our training curriculum, leverage the new tripartite Jobs Council and create pathways that attract our young graduates into these new and exciting roles.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us match our young graduates' interests and aptitudes early, while they are still in school, to career ramps available in aviation, logistics and maritime.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And let us ensure that the work conditions and prospects, particularly at the entry level, can genuinely attract and retain our younger workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of them need to see their future potential, beyond the internship and the traineeship period, that, if they work hard, there are real prospects for progression – to move into higher value roles, with better wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us double down on our efforts so that we can see more young Singaporeans grow and flourish alongside the development of the transport sector.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of them will see their daily tasks change with technology.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must identify at-risk roles early, map them to adjacent opportunities and build career pathways.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we get this right, transformation becomes a story of renewal and of growth, not about replacement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, we must also redesign jobs alongside our workers to help them see how technology can help them to get their jobs done better.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And we must provide our workers the necessary support and training pathways to help them move into higher-value, better jobs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond wages and work prospects, it is also important to ensure that jobs in the transport sector also provide better welfare and better working conditions for our workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Worker welfare must also include safety, especially for workers whose duties expose them to the heat, thunderstorms and other adverse weather conditions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This matters in transport, where aviation, maritime, logistics and port workers continue to keep operations running on the ground, at our terminals, at sea and on the tarmac.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we transform our transport sector, we must apply these technologies more directly to protect our workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us leverage technology to support efforts to plan rostering, shifts and rest hours more thoughtfully, especially to support round-the-clock operations in our transport sector.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we build world-class infrastructure, let us also ensure that we plan for adequate amenities for our workers who have to work onsite – affordable food, good rest facilities and quiet rooms for long shifts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope to see more of such amenities provided for our workers onsite.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, by deploying AVs to enable first- and last-mile connections to Changi, Tuas, our ferry terminals and our industrial estates.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These work sites generally have less access to public transportation, especially in the early and late hours.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We should know who are entering these new roles and whether our young graduates, rank-and-file workers and technicians are benefiting.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Such tracking can help monitor worker composition, training outcomes, wage progression and career mobility so that transformation remains accountable to our workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: An aspect of welfare for our workers is also one that we tend to forget is the word “respect”.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Every time there is a rail breakdown, public frustration is immediate and often directed at them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But what many of us do not see is their reality – working through the night, managing complex systems, carrying the responsibility of keeping millions of commuters safe.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This reminds us that strengthening our transport hub is not just about better systems.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about valuing the people behind them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we want the next generation to join such jobs, the jobs must be stable and well-paying too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But at the end of the day, respect is important. :   Mr Speaker, please allow me to speak briefly in Malay.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When we talk about the future of transport, it is not just about technology or efficiency.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Within the transport sector, new opportunities will certainly emerge.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But those opportunities will not materialise if information is unclear, training is not aligned with real jobs, and support does not reach workers early enough.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is why we need to build career bridges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not just about more courses, but a clear pathway that connects skills to jobs, and jobs to better lives.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, allow me to conclude with three asks, or three calls.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Better wages, better welfare and better work prospects.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, every Singaporean, our youth and our rank-and-file workers, can see, can enter and progress in these opportunities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our ambition must be to become a people-centred transport hub, where growth creates good jobs, technology uplifts our workers and every Singaporean has a pathway forward.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Because in the end, a hub is only as strong as its people.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Behind every successful transport hub are workers whose skills, whose commitment and professionalism keep Singapore moving.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And when our workers move forward with confidence, Singapore will continue to move forward too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As an international economist who has spent the better part of his professional career teaching and advocating for the virtues of free trade, economic integration and technological forwardness, I am both deeply encouraged and keenly vested in the spirit of this Motion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alas, it behooves me to point out that the world has, if anything, been moving in the opposite direction, with the erosion of globalisation, a retreat from liberal international organisation and a shift toward policy-making informed by geopolitical might and domestic populist pressures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will therefore speak today about a tail risk – how to manage our cross-border economic policy and international relations in the face of a de-globalising world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The risk has been slowly manifesting itself ever more vividly over the course of the past two decades, as the global policy landscape has evolved from the 20th century rules-based order toward the 21st century law of the jungle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, I do not do so as an alarmist, but as a realist.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if a wholesale move in this direction seems remote, we must gird our collective loins and formulate policy that is grounded in the emerging reality of a world where flows of goods, services, capital, labour and technology might face ever greater frictions in their movement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, while I support the overall thrust of this Motion, I encourage this House to also be clear-eyed about a potential downside scenario.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To fully understand this, we must look backward to the Global Financial Crisis of 2007/2008, and more recently to the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the causes are still being debated, the consequences are already clear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The capricious deployment of tariffs and other commercial policy instruments have also resulted in a trade map aligned more toward geopolitical affiliation, rather than economic logic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Cross-border capital flows have similarly stagnated after the crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This reverses the heady times of ever-rising financial integration, which took flight in the 1980s.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The slowdown has likewise led some to speculate that we are entering into an era of financial de-globalisation, where international finance will become increasingly fragmented and controlled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The trends of friend-shoring and rising economic nationalism also suggest that foreign investment will perhaps be far less forthcoming in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Through all this, the flow of workers between countries has remained robust.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If anything, advances in digital connectivity have flattened the world, promoting the outsourcing of tasks between countries and encouraging the globalisation of labour, both unskilled and skilled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Falling transportation costs also spurred an unprecedented rise in tourism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The pandemic, alas, struck the first blow on this front.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And while migratory flows have rebounded somewhat, they have been repeatedly threatened by rising geopolitical tensions and global conflict.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some believe that information and communication technologies will allow digital flows to substitute for the decline in these other channels of globalisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, while we are reasonably assured that connectivity will be sustained along this dimension, it has not been unvarnished by geopolitical pressures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The ban on advanced AI hardware by the US is but one reflection of renewed restrictions, along with the disabling of the most advanced AI models to foreign nationals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As the Economic Strategy Review Committee has observed, we also do not possess the capability to build our own foundational AI models.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus, even as we strengthen our national AI strategy, it is clear that we are vulnerable to being disintermediated in an AI-led world economy, in both hardware as well as software.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unfortunately, the decline in international exchange has been accompanied by an erosion of international cooperation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Treaties are being repeatedly re-negotiated and international organisations struggle to retain their traditional voice of authority in global fora.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Instead, governance is dominated by fears of political polarisation and popular sentiment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The world is becoming increasingly multipolar, and the conduct of international trade and finance appear to be driven much more by politics than economic fundamentals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Increasingly, economic tools are also being deployed to meet geopolitical objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This model has served us well, and we have relied on our openness and status as a trusted intermediary to build an economy that is among the richest in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I fear that the new global order will be far less accommodating to business as usual.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With a slowing in international exchange of goods, we need to pivot towards services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We must foster more growth in tradable services, which has the added benefit that it is also less subjected to the need to undervalue our exchange rate as a policy, since services are much more likely to be competitive on the basis of quality and efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if we are indeed focused on trade and services, we should keep in mind that we export more to the European Union (EU) than the US, and more to ASEAN than to China.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We also should not expect our trade orientation to be remain global in nature, rather than regional.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This does not mean prematurely surrendering our entrepôt status, it does mean taking our economic relationships with our near abroad – Asia, in general; and ASEAN, in particular, much more seriously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should regard Southeast Asia as our hinterland, producing for that broader market and wean ourselves of trade that is focused much more on the West.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will position us better in a world that is more multipolar and regional, as opposed to unipolar and global.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This also implies that we should rethink how much time and effort we spend on trade facilitation with partners, like the US.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, as my hon friends, Gerald Giam and Kenneth Tiong, both pointed out, heavily placing our bets on mega-sized physical infrastructure projects, such as Changi T5 and the Tuas Next Generation Port may backfire if globalisation is more restrained in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This does not mean that we turn inward on these projects or abandon them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The same will apply to our long-term infrastructure borrowing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So long as the parts that are built are fully self-contained, we can adopt a more incrementalist approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The same applies to capital flows, where we should look to investing more in the region.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unlike our early days, where we were starved of capital, we now have large public and private funds that can direct our considerable net national savings elsewhere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the national will to provide such guidance remains unclear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Look, for instance, at our nation's foreign direct investment (FDI).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While it is perhaps unsurprising that China and India top the list of FDI partners, the next ones on the list are the United Kingdom, Indonesia, Australia and the US.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Among our top FDI destinations, only two, Indonesia and Malaysia, are in ASEAN.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The argument is also relevant from the sell-side perspective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As we strive to cement our position as an international financial centre, we must also recognise and accept that economies, like China, the EU and the US, are increasingly likely to favour financial intermediation through their own onshore locales, like Shanghai or Hong Kong; London or Frankfurt; New York or Chicago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should instead appeal to regional businesses and attract them, and not just American entities to list on the Singapore Exchange, and to encourage them to park their buy-side wealth management operations here, rather than elsewhere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The re-alignment of focus applies to labour flows too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, we are already highly integrated when it comes to absorbing low-cost workers from the region.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Through Enterprise SG, we already have an analogous scheme – the Global Ready Talent Programme – that encourages companies to train young talent through overseas internships.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This should not be limited to early-career professionals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relocation costs can be minimised perhaps with state acquisition of properties that can be rented out to Singaporean firms at attractive rates, especially SMEs looking to internationalise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I had also shared that international schools can be made more plug-and-play for relocating families with subsidised fees similar to what is offered at home and stronger syllabus coordination to make the return much more seamless.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This can and should be corrected and all the more in the world where PMETs in other regional countries are converging, on our own in terms of training, skills and experience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Next, if we accept the premise that digital and virtual exchange will increasingly substitute for the other traditional modes of trading goods, services, capital and labour, then the ability to exert control or at least exert leverage over access to the underlying technological infrastructure becomes far more critical.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is the case for both hardware – and here, I am thinking about data centres, in particular – and software, in terms of foundational AI models, whether applied through generative, agentic or embodied cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My party colleagues, Dennis Tan and Gerald Giam, argued in favour of expanding our ownership over these tools to build our nation's digital resilience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the rest of the world may not agree.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Otherwise, we might find ourselves unable to strike deals at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, allow me to close with a football analogy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Players and seasoned fans will know that when pressing a counterattack, one does not pass to where the other players are now, but to where the other players might be going.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: From my vantage point, on the field's left wing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Otherwise, we may find ourselves inadvertently off-side, and our economy and society left out in the cold.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have been in the Chamber for close to five hours.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.19 pm until 3.40 pm.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: But this position cannot be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
